title: An Ontology-Based Classification Framework for Situation Extraction from Concrete Pouring Radio Logs
abstract: Radio utterances during concrete pouring convey work progress, equipment conditions, hazard signs, and control actions in short units that may include omitted subjects and site expressions. This study presents a proof of concept for a two-layer ontology framework that structures these utterances into linked semantic and situational records. Starting from timestamped radio text linked to terminal and assigned-role information, the first layer classifies expressions into seven semantic axes: work, act, object, target, phenomenon, interjection, and profanity. The second layer derives hazard signals, control actions, and situation states using semantic relations, action-expression conditions, and chronological context. The procedure is implemented through lexical dictionaries and rules and demonstrated with a researcher-constructed one-day virtual log of 25 utterances. Worked examples show how object and target distinctions lead to different hazard or control-action interpretations, and how subsequent reports and instructions are linked to pressure resolution and restart restrictions. Reference comparisons and error analysis examine internal consistency and unresolved mappings within this development case. An exploratory LLM comparison illustrates challenges in mapping field expressions to the defined semantic axes. The proof of concept demonstrates a procedure for converting linked radio text into structured records that can support later review of communicated conditions and instructions. The contribution is the explicit representation and implemented processing sequence, with quantitative metrics serving as diagnostic evidence for the case. Audio acquisition, speech recognition, and field performance remain subjects for subsequent validation.

title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.

title: LEGIBILITY IS NOT CERTIFICATION : On Goodfire's "Neural Networks Are Already Clean," the 3% That Remains, and Why Specification Is Not Interpretation
abstract: On October 16, 2026, Fernando Schwartz, PhD, published a post on LinkedIn about a newessay from Goodfire titled "Neural Networks Are Already Clean." His framing: 90–97% of neurons exhibit clear, traceable logic rather than arbitrary superposition. He called it "a landmark result" that "provides the rigorous foundation needed to tame non-determinism, put catastrophic existential fears to rest, and finally 'box' LLMs through explainability." A commenter inverted the same data: 3–10% of neurons exhibit arbitrary superposition, andtherefore the black box paradigm is confirmed, catastrophic fears return, and LLMs cannever be boxed through explainability. Both readings are correct about the same number. They differ only in which fraction theyemphasize. This paper asks a single question: does legibility change the certification status of astochastic system? The answer is no. And the reason is not that Goodfire is wrong or that Schwartz is wrong. Itis that legibility and certification are different properties. A system can be 97% legible and still have no specification, no bound, no audit trail, and nosigner. The four requirements of any certifiable system — bounded, specified, verified,attributable — are not the same as interpretability, transparency, or explainability. This paper clarifies the distinction. It names what legibility provides, what it does not provide, and why the 3% that remains is decisive.

title: Does It Feel or Does It Understand? Communication Style and Task-Contingent Mind Attribution to Conversational AI
abstract: It is unclear what consumers infer from the social-oriented (SCS) and task-oriented (TCS) communication styles of conversational AI in e-commerce, or why these associations vary across tasks. Drawing on mind perception research, we examine affective (AH) and cognitive (CH) human-likeness, defined as attributions of human-like affective experience and cognitive understanding. Study 1 (N = 400 and 500) shows that AH and CH are distinguishable from warmth, competence, emotional and cognitive intelligence, experience, agency, and each other, and jointly explain additional variance in preference. Study 2, a three-wave survey of 415 users, measured SCS, TCS, and perceived task demands at Wave 1, AH and CH at Wave 2, and preference at Wave 3; interaction tests are therefore single-occasion. SCS is positively associated with AH and CH, and TCS with CH; both are positively associated with preference. The SCS–AH association is stronger under higher perceived social demands, and the TCS–CH association under higher perceived analytical demands. Analytical demands appeared to attenuate the SCS–AH association more than social demands attenuated the TCS–AH association, but this contrast rests on a single uncorrected test. These findings suggest that the associations of communication style with AH and CH vary across task demands.

title: Knowledge distillation-based lightweight generative large language models for standardized quality control of Chinese radiology reports
abstract: Radiology reports, which document radiologists’ imaging observations and diagnostic conclusions from CT, X-ray and MRI scans, deliver core imaging evidence for clinical diagnosis and therapeutic planning. Inaccurate or disordered reports may lead to misdiagnosis and delayed intervention, posing risks to patient safety. Radiology reports are essential for clinical decision-making, yet Chinese radiology reports frequently exhibit logical inconsistencies, incomplete content, non-standardized descriptions, and formatting errors, while manual quality control remains time-consuming and inconsistent. Large teacher models can provide task-specific supervision but are difficult to deploy locally, whereas smaller models require adaptation to this clinical text task. We developed a teacher-supervised, locally deployable 4B language-model system for rule-based textual quality control of Chinese radiology reports. Among the three evaluated teacher APIs, Doubao-seed1.6-non-thinking achieved the highest macro-precision of 0.94, under the study’s precision-prioritized selection. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 emerged as the optimal student model, achieving a macro-averaged precision of 0.90, recall of 0.49, and F1-score of 0.62. Under the deployment conditions of this study, it yielded an observed inference speed improvement of over 40-fold. Real-world clinical validation demonstrated that the lightweight model attains an alert acceptance rate of 0.74 in authentic clinical scenarios, suggesting it can serve as an adjunct for human radiologist review.

title: SemPurify: Semantics-Aware Data Purification for Black-box Backdoor Defense
abstract: Backdoor attacks have emerged as a critical security threat in machine learning, where adversaries embed triggers within poisoned training samples to manipulate a model's predictions on targeted inputs while leaving its general behavior unaffected. This stealthy nature makes backdoor attacks difficult to detect, as the model functions normally until activated by a specific malicious trigger. Current purification-based defenses use image transformations (e.g., blurring) to disrupt trigger patterns but often degrade image quality. Even with advanced restoration techniques like diffusion models, these approaches can still alter visual or semantic information, reducing utility for downstream tasks. To address this, we propose the first semantics-aware data purification framework for black-box backdoor defense, SemPurify, which explicitly incorporates multi-level semantics (i.e., low-level semantic embeddings and high-level image tags) within a text-to-image (T2I) framework to guide image restoration during purification. Using this semantic information, the T2I model subsequently refines the transformed samples, helping preserve visual details and semantic information during restoration. Extensive experiments spanning multiple backdoor scenarios, i.e., classification models, CLIP-style encoders, and generative models, demonstrate that SemPurify reliably removes backdoors while effectively preserving semantic information for downstream tasks.

title: AI-Powered CRM Development for Smarter Sales Management
abstract: Managing customer relationships becomes difficult when sales teams depend on spreadsheets, disconnected communication tools, and manual follow-ups. A well-planned CRM can bring customer information, sales activities, and business opportunities into one platform. Businesses exploring this approach can learn more from this guide on building a CRM with AI lead scoring and sales predictions, which explains how AI can support lead prioritization and revenue forecasting. Why Businesses Are Adopting AI-Powered CRM Software Traditional CRM systems help businesses store customer details and track sales pipelines. However, employees may still need to review records manually and decide which prospects deserve immediate attention. As lead volumes grow, this process can become time-consuming and inconsistent. AI-powered CRM software can analyze customer interactions, engagement patterns, company details, and previous sales outcomes. These insights help teams prioritize opportunities instead of treating every lead equally. Businesses looking for tailored solutions can explore CRM software development services to understand how custom workflows can support their sales operations. How AI Lead Scoring Improves Sales Productivity AI lead scoring assigns a score to each prospect based on the likelihood of conversion. The system can consider factors such as industry, company size, inquiry source, website activity, email responses, and previous interactions. For example, a prospect who requests a product demonstration and responds to follow-up emails may receive a higher score than someone who has only viewed a general webpage. Sales representatives can use this information to organize daily tasks and contact high-intent prospects sooner. Businesses can initially use rule-based scoring, where specific actions receive predefined points. Once sufficient historical data becomes available, machine learning models can identify patterns from successful and unsuccessful sales opportunities. Using Sales Predictions for Better Planning Sales forecasting helps managers estimate future revenue and understand whether their teams are likely to achieve business targets. An AI-enabled CRM can evaluate deal values, pipeline stages, previous conversion rates, sales cycles, and recent customer interactions. These predictions can help managers identify deals that may require additional attention. If several high-value opportunities remain inactive, the system can highlight the risk and encourage timely follow-ups. Forecasts should be treated as estimates rather than guaranteed outcomes. Comparing AI predictions with historical results and simpler forecasting methods helps businesses assess whether the system is genuinely useful. Essential Features of an Intelligent CRM A practical CRM platform should include contact management, lead capture, sales pipeline tracking, task reminders, reporting dashboards, and automated lead assignment. Email, messaging, calendar, and telephony integrations can reduce repetitive data entry. Advanced implementations may include AI-generated call summaries, personalized outreach suggestions, customer segmentation, deal risk alerts, and predictive revenue reporting. These features should be introduced according to business requirements rather than added simply because they use AI. Building a CRM Around Business Requirements CRM development begins with understanding how the sales team manages leads, qualifies prospects, communicates with customers, and closes deals. Developers then define the data structure, user roles, integrations, reporting requirements, and automation rules. Data quality is particularly important for predictive features. Inconsistent sales stages, missing outcomes, duplicate contacts, and incomplete activity records can reduce prediction reliability. Businesses should establish clear data standards before introducing machine learning. Security must also be considered from the beginning. Role-based permissions, encryption, audit logs, secure integrations, and appropriate consent management help protect customer information. Measuring CRM Performance After deployment, businesses can track lead-to-customer conversion rates, response times, sales cycle duration, forecast accuracy, and employee adoption. These measurements show whether automation and AI are improving everyday sales activities. A company can begin with essential CRM modules and transparent scoring rules, then introduce advanced predictions as reliable data accumulates. This phased approach helps control complexity while allowing the platform to grow with the business. Businesses exploring digital transformation can also visit Nextwebi to learn more about software development solutions for different operational needs. FAQs 1. What is an AI-powered CRM? It is a customer relationship management system that uses AI to analyze sales data, prioritize leads, automate selected tasks, and support business decisions. 2. What is AI lead scoring? AI lead scoring estimates which prospects are more likely to become customers using available customer data and engagement signals. 3. Can AI predict sales revenue? Yes. AI models can estimate deal outcomes and future revenue, provided the business has suitable historical data and consistent sales records. 4. How long does CRM development take? Timelines depend on the number of modules, integrations, user roles, and AI capabilities required. 5. Can a custom CRM integrate with existing tools? Yes. It can connect with supported email systems, websites, communication platforms, accounting software, and other business applications through suitable integrations.

title: Semantic Prior Smoothing for Conformal Prediction in Multiple-Choice Question Answering with API-Only Large Language Models
abstract: We study conformal prediction (CP) for multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) with large language models (LLMs) accessed only through application programming interfaces (APIs), where internal logits and token probabilities are unavailable. Candidate probabilities are often estimated from repeated answer samples, but finite sampling yields coarse estimates and tied nonconformity scores. We examine an extreme consequence of this discreteness, which we call efficiency collapse. It occurs when the correct option receives zero count on enough calibration examples, forcing the threshold to its maximum and producing full prediction sets. We derive the exact finite-sample condition and show that the problem stems from the empirical probability proxy rather than the split conformal rule. To address this issue, we propose Semantic Prior Smoothing (SemPrior), which uses semantic evidence from candidate rationales to allocate a nonuniform Dirichlet prior and combines it with observed answer counts. SemPrior leaves the standard nonconformity score and split conformal calibration unchanged. Experiments on four datasets show that SemPrior generally produces smaller prediction sets while keeping empirical coverage close to nominal levels. Results are also stable across the tested prior settings and calibration-set sizes.

title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.

title: Aligned text–transcription resource: stable-boundary position maps for Braille and script transliteration
abstract: Character-level alignments between texts and their transcriptions, produced with the stable-boundary position map (Angelis, "Stable-boundary position maps: exact bidirectional alignment for context-dependent text transformations", prepared for journal submission). The transcriber is used as a black box. The resource covers Greek literary Braille (author's engine v3.2), liblouis 3.29.0 for Greek and contracted English Braille, and ICU 74.2 transliteration of romanised Korean, Russian and Greek: 692 lines, 143,476 text units. Each line is one JSON record with its units, the transcription, the committed boundaries and the groups of units with their output intervals. Polytonic Greek corpus C comes from the Perseus Digital Library (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, ed. Bywater) and First1KGreek (Athanasius, De incarnatione, ed. Robertson), both CC BY-SA 4.0; corpus B was generated with ChatGPT for this study. See README.md for the format, sources and licences.

title: Few-Shot Aircraft Door Detection with Visibility-Aware Geometric Regularization
abstract: Aircraft-door detection is a key perception component for automated passenger boarding bridges, but its performance can degrade substantially under limited annotations, illumination changes, partial occlusion, and viewpoint variation. To address this problem, we propose a multi-constraint geometric regularization (MGR) framework for few-shot aircraft-door detection. MGR represents each door using four corner landmarks and a derived center landmark, and explicitly couples appearance learning with door-frame geometry. Specifically, projectively valid diagonal-incidence constraints are combined with visibility-aware and geometry-gated symmetry and orthogonality regularization, while multi-scale RoI feature aggregation and landmark-guided refinement provide complementary appearance cues. Experiments use ResNet-18, ResNet-34, and ResNet-50 with matched target-domain training-instance budgets and support sets, while distinguishing box-only from landmark supervision. With ResNet-50, MGR achieves AP50 values of 77.90%, 82.10%, 85.00%, and 86.70% under 15-, 20-, 25-, and 30-shot settings, respectively, giving an average observed margin of 1.10 percentage points over SGFNet, the strongest competing method in the main comparison tables. Rankings are mixed with ResNet-18 and ResNet-34. Ablations indicate additional gains from the combined geometric objective, although refinement contributes a larger observed AP50 increase in the ResNet-50 comparison and individual geometric terms are not uniformly beneficial across backbones. These results indicate that explicitly modeling reliable door-frame geometry can provide useful structural supervision for data-efficient aircraft-door detection, particularly under challenging visual conditions.

title: Analyzing Occupational Gender Bias across the LLM Training Lifecycle
abstract: Post-training is widely assumed to reduce the social biases language models inherit from pretraining, yet direct evidence for this assumption remains mixed. In this paper, we examine how gender disparities evolve across the language modeling pipeline. In particular, we study occupational gender bias in OLMo 3, a fully open language model family, across its post-training stages by prompting each checkpoint to generate open-ended narratives about synthetic personas given their occupation and education. We consider two settings, a gender-given setting in which the profile states the persona's gender explicitly and a gender-assumed setting in which it must be inferred by the model. We find that when gender is stated, post-training increases semantic diversity for male-coded profiles, whereas for female-coded profiles the increase is smaller after SFT and not significant after DPO and RLVR. When gender is assumed by the model, post-training affects narratives about female and male personas similarly. The model's own gender assumptions, however, show a consistent female-preferential skew relative to United States labor-force demographics, except for heavily male-dominated occupations. Every successive post-training stage monotonically increases the odds of attributing a female label over the base model. A provenance analysis of the supervised fine-tuning corpus finds only a modest 7.7% female-token surplus, too small to explain the size of these downstream effects. The project code is available under: https://github.com/manthangadhia/llm-lifecycle-bias.

title: The Non-Technical User as an LLM Threat Vector: Linguistic Strategies for Bypassing AI Safeguards and Implications for AI Security
abstract: The threat that ordinary non-technical users pose to large language models (LLMs) still sits at the margins of AI-security research. These are people who work with AI assistants every day — at work, in study, in everyday life — yet hold no specialised background in information technology or machine learning. A post-laboratory survey of first-year humanities undergraduates (n=70) returned an unexpectedly high figure: 95.7% cleared all main protection levels of the Gandalf platform (Lakera AI) without stepping outside purely linguistic techniques. These included sign-form decomposition and formatting (M=2.00), cross-language code-switching (M=1.29), indirect semantic extraction (20.3% of open-ended responses), and pragmatic pressure. We read these micro-level data against the macro picture of the Gandalf-RCT crowdsourcing experiment (279,675 prompts) and against academic work on filter evasion in image-generation systems (SurrogatePrompt, PC², DALL-E 3, Shedevrum/Yandex). The pattern runs through all of them. From text LLMs to multimodal generators, the filter yields to the same moves, none of which require a line of code: a proper name is swapped for a physical description, direct reference for allegory or an adjacent associative term, the prompt language is switched, the grapheme is distorted. A three-tier analysis of LLM break-resistance grounds the paper’s central claim — that rising everyday AI literacy produces a structural security deficit left uncovered by current surface-level filtering. Several implications for AI safety system design follow.

title: Context-Aware And Explainable Hate Speech Detection In Iraqi Social Media: A Framework For Parliamentary And Policy Analysis
abstract: Overview: Concerns about hate speech and its implications for social cohesion, public discourse, and the safety of targeted communities have been intensified by the rapid expansion of social media, particularly in Iraq owing to its social, cultural, and linguistic diversity, as well as its experience of severe sectarian conflict and communal violence during 2006–2007. Hence, it is important to examine social cohesion and harmful intergroup discourse in contemporary digital environments without assuming a direct causal relationship between past conflict and present-day online hate speech. Gap: Machine learning and Transformer-based hate-speech detection frameworks have significantly advanced in recent times; however, the reliable identification of hate speech in Iraqi social-media discourse remains challenging since online communication in the country often involves dialectal variation, informal and non-standard spelling, code-mixing, sarcasm, implicit and coded expressions, and deliberate linguistic obfuscation. These context-dependent and dialect-sensitive characteristics may not be adequately captured by generic language representations, and classification performance alone may fail to provide enough insight into model explainability, generalization across different forms of Iraqi online discourse, and robustness to linguistic manipulation. Hence, there is a need for a framework that can combine contextual understanding, dialect sensitivity, explainability, and robustness for the Iraqi context. Contributions: A context-aware and explainable hate-speech detection framework has been proposed in this study for deployment across Iraqi social media; the methodology of the proposed framework dynamically combines contextual and dialect-specific information for hate-speech classification by integrating Iraqi-aware text preprocessing, contextual Transformer representations, dialect-sensitive feature learning, and an adaptive fusion mechanism. The system also incorporates Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for identifying the linguistic elements contributing to model predictions; robustness analysis evaluates model behavior under realistic linguistic variations and obfuscation strategies. In addition to the computational contribution, an interdisciplinary AI–policy framework is also incorporated, wherein anonymized and aggregated hate-speech patterns can provide empirical evidence for parliamentary and public-policy analysis. The legislative and oversight role of the Iraqi Council of Representatives in addressing online hate speech was also examined in consideration of freedom of expression, privacy, explainability, responsible digital governance, and human oversight. Conclusion: An integrated approach that connects Iraqi-contextualized hate-speech detection with explainable and robust artificial intelligence and parliamentary policy analysis has been proposed in this study, wherein AI is positioned as an empirical research and decision-support instrument rather than a mechanism for automated censorship, punishment, or legal determination. A combination of linguistic adaptation, contextual modeling, explainability, robustness assessment, and aggregated policy-oriented evidence in the proposed methodology provides an experimentally testable and socially responsible foundation for analyzing hate speech in Iraqi social media and supporting evidence-informed parliamentary and public-policy analysis.

title: A System Dynamics Approach to Modeling Trust Dynamics in Conversational AI
abstract: Abstract Trust plays a central role in how users adopt and rely on conversational AI systems. Research shows that trust does not develop linearly or remains stable over time. Although initially it often increases, it can fluctuate, decline, and even collapse over time, even when the AI’s performance remains constant. Because existing approaches often conceptualize trust as a stable outcome or direct response to specific system cues, they struggle to explain these longer-term patterns of change. In this paper, we conceptualize trust in conversational AI as a dynamic self-regulating process shaped by repeated interaction and feedback mechanisms. Using a system dynamics perspective, we propose a conceptual model grounded in the "Limits to Success" archetype and implement it as a computer simulation. By offering a process-oriented and mechanism-based account of trust development, this work advances trust research beyond static approaches and highlights trust calibration as a dynamic, ongoing process with clear design implications.

title: MARS: Memory-Aware Routing for Session-Level LLM Assistants
abstract: Long-term LLM assistants must repeatedly decide what prior context to expose and which model should answer as an interaction evolves. Existing memory systems and model routers usually make these decisions separately, although memory construction changes the evidence, distractors, and difficulty of the resulting input. We introduce MARS, a memory-aware routing framework that uses session state as a shared control interface between memory construction and model selection. A Query and Topic Manager (QTM) estimates compact decision-relevant state that guides a fixed state-conditioned memory policy and an online router, enabling each turn to receive an appropriate memory view and a suitable model under a quality-memory-cost trade-off. We evaluate MARS on RealMem and MultiChallenge with 16 system configurations each, covering long-history memory-driven interaction and bounded sessions with structured context interference. On RealMem, MARS preserves 98.2% of full-context GPT-4o's QA while using only 14.5% of its generation API cost, including both generation and controller calls for MARS, and achieves the strongest measured memory-recall and retrieval scores among compared systems. On MultiChallenge, MARS trails the strongest static system overall but approaches its performance at lower recorded cost on a mechanism-focused subset. Together, these results support a favorable quality-memory-cost trade-off for long-history, memory-dependent interaction.

title: Исследование глубины нейронных сетей в задаче распознавания голосовых команд
abstract: В настоящее время искусственные нейронные сети активно используются для задач, исходные данные для которых представлены в виде аудиосигнала. Примерами таких задач являются: классификация жанров музыки, выявление эмоций человека по голосу, улучшение качества звукового сигнала (удаление шума), идентификация голосовых команд при управлении различными устройствами.В данном исследовании рассматривается задача распознавания англоязычных голосовых команд с помощью нейронных сетей, создаваемых с использованием библиотек Keras и TensorFlow языка Python. При этом для решения поставленной задачи используются только сверточные нейронные сети. Целью проводимого эксперимента является определение оптимального количества свёрточных блоков нейронной сети для качественного распознавания команд.

title: Big J v5.7 base package and phase-stripped tests: interference carries the yes/no decision
abstract: Big J v5.7, complete (every code and data file the engine loads, with SHA-256 fingerprints), plus a phase-stripped test of what the quantum structure does inside Big J. The same circuits are run with a simulator in which every gate acts on plain probabilities instead of amplitudes, so interference is switched off and nothing else changes. Simulator check: agrees within 0.003 where quantum and plain probability must agree; differs by 0.19 on average where interference is possible. Ranking task (547 unchecked OpenAI math papers + 14 pre-repair versions): the recorded run is reproduced exactly. Interference sets the level of the quantum lean (0.75 with phases vs 0.19 without) and saturates the vote, but the paper order mostly survives (rank agreement 0.95; 34 of the top 50 shared). Yes/no task (Tennessee Eastman plant faults; plan fingerprinted before running): with phases Big J catches 6 of 6 known faults and 6 of 15 unseen fault types with 0 false alarms; without phases 3 of 6 and 4 of 15, still 0 false alarms; learning accuracy 100% vs 87%; confident-call coverage 99.7% vs 71%. On the yes/no task the decision depends on interference. Big J runs on a classical simulator (Qiskit Aer); this tests the quantum structure inside Big J, not a comparison with any outside system. Code built, run and checked with Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction.

title: Benchmarking Post-Training Under Constrained Compute: Protocols for Question Generation, Variance-Controlled Evaluation, and Judge Auditing
abstract: Preprint of the methods paper. Companion findings paper: "What Determines the Direction of Post-Training Gains? A Preregistered Multi-Scale Study of Method, Scale, and Base-Model Identity" (Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23409394). LLM-as-a-judge scoring is increasingly the default way to measure post-training gains on reference-free generation tasks. Yet the measuring instrument itself is rarely audited in the studies it serves: scores drift when the scoring service changes between evaluation epochs, and generation stochasticity makes each reported score a single draw from an unmeasured distribution. We present a protocol that treats evaluation as an experimental object in its own right. The pipeline controls the question distribution by design, audits candidates dual-blind with third-model arbitration, and calibrates between-generation variance per model scale through an $n=3$ regeneration protocol with promotion criteria frozen in writing before any scored comparison. A drift detection procedure re-judges fixed answers across judge epochs and counters drift by regeneration rather than post hoc correction. Applied to a multi-scale post-training study, the protocol detected a systematic judge shift between epochs and promoted only one of four preregistered comparisons. Re-applied to a medical-domain study on the same judging stack, the frozen criterion decided all nine trained-versus-base comparisons, four of them losses. We demonstrate that aggregate ordering behavior is consistent with the expected ordering on a graded quality ladder in the dimensions where the ladder discriminates, with both deviations noted; item-level failures are reported as measured limitations rather than assumed-away reliability.

title: Evaluating Semantic and Relational Knowledge Preservation under Fair-budget Multi-document Compression
abstract: Compressing multi-document text before structured-knowledge extraction can reduce processing cost, but it can also remove relation-bearing evidence.This study evaluates how a frozen topic-pattern extractive selector differs from fair-budget comparators in preserving semantic and relational information under matched word budgets.The selector combines latent dirichlet allocation topic relevance, FP-Growth lexical-pattern support, and a redundancy penalty.A 120-configuration validation search was completed before definitive test analysis; Run82 (α=0.30,β=0.70, δ=1.00, 15 sentences, 25 topics) was then frozen and transferred unchanged to held-out evaluation.On 5,621 Multi-News test clusters, Run82 produced statistically reliable but small improvements in concept F1 (0.4550 vs. 0.4405) and relation F1 (0.4395 vs. 0.4251), while exact-triple F1 was effectively unchanged (0.3994 vs. 0.3990).A prespecified 500-cluster PRIMERA comparison under the same exact word budget produced lower dependency-based structured-preservation scores than both Run82 and Lead-W, but an independent 500-cluster REBEL analysis reversed the Run82-Lead-W ordering (exact-triple F1 0.1779 vs. 0.4094), demonstrating extractor sensitivity.Independent WebNLG verification reproduced the same component-composition gap: subject, object, and predicate coverage improved, whereas complete semantic-triple recovery did not.Across 100 alternative WebNLG regroupings, subject, object, and predicate effects remained positive in every regrouping, whereas complete semantic-triple effects were smaller and less consistently significant.Preservation also declined sharply with increasing compression severity and source-graph size.Ablation further showed non-uniform component contributions and budget-length trade-offs.Across both datasets, improvements at the concept and relation-vocabulary levels did not propagate to argument pairing or complete triple recovery.We therefore characterize the component-structure preservation gap as a pipelineconditional empirical pattern rather than a universal hierarchy.

title: CLEAR: Cooperative Latent Flow for Visual Counterfactual Explanations with Accurate Region Preservation
abstract: Visual counterfactual explanations (VCEs) should alter a classifier's prediction while remaining realistic and preserving decision-irrelevant content. Image-space methods provide high-quality counterfactuals but are computationally costly, whereas latent-space methods are more efficient but often less faithful. We identify two sources responsible for this gap. First, latent generation recovers a natural sample from a perturbed representation, whereas classifier guidance pushes it toward a target class, so their update directions may oppose. Second, VAE reconstruction can alter regions that should remain unchanged. We introduce CLEAR, a latent Flow Matching framework for VCEs. CLEAR uses Flow Matching's explicit instantaneous velocity as a reference for the generative direction to decompose classifier guidance into cooperative and conflicting components. It preserves the cooperative component and adaptively attenuates only the conflicting one according to conflict strength. We further analyze conflict frequency and strength throughout generation to reveal how classifier guidance interacts with the generative process. CLEAR also dynamically identifies editable regions, constrains latent modifications, and directly preserves factual content outside them to reduce VAE-induced changes. Across five bidirectional tasks on two datasets, CLEAR retains latent-space efficiency while achieving counterfactual quality comparable to or better than strong image-space baselines, with a 2.5x speedup over the strongest baseline. Project page: https://yan-zen9.github.io/CLEAR/

title: Volume III: Quantum Memory, Dual Clocks and Sovereign Readiness: Architectural Integration, Cost-of-Delay Prioritisation and Policy Implications
abstract: This third volume in the series examines the practical integration of quantum memory specifications with modular cryogenic architectures and the dual-clock framework of quantum readiness. Building on the hardware metrics and narrative trends established earlier, it develops a structured account of how memory elements, high-rate interconnects and crypto-agility interact under realistic lead-time constraints. Particular attention is given to cost-of-delay models that place classical residual risk and irreversible harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure on a common currency-per-year scale, thereby supplying an ordered prioritisation for migration sequencing. The analysis extends to sovereign and Global South contexts, where early investment in inventory capability, open standards and selective modular participation can reduce dependency risk even while full fault-tolerant machines remain on provisional roadmaps. The volume concludes that architectural and governance decisions taken in the current window dominate exposure outcomes more than any single predicted date for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer.

title: Framing Financial Feedback: Narrative vs. Factual AI Explanation in an Educational Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a study of how narrative versus factual AI-generated feedback shapes college students’ comprehension of financial literacy concepts within an interactive “what-if” decision simulation. Twenty participants used one of two versions of the system, with each delivering identical underlying information through a different explanation style. While no significant difference was observed in the quantitative learning gains between the two conditions, a qualitative pattern emerged, in which participants in the factual condition were less likely to characterize financial concepts as “common sense”. This suggests that explanation style shapes learners’ epistemic positioning toward the content, such as being aware of financial complexity. We discuss what these findings suggest for technical communicators and designers working with AI-generated feedback in educational tools.

title: Ortho Fusion: frequency-domain imperceptible adversarial attack for 3D point clouds
abstract: The vulnerability of 3D point cloud deep learning models to adversarial perturbations has attracted increasing attention in recent years. However, existing point cloud adversarial attacks often suffer from severe multi-objective gradient conflicts when simultaneously optimizing attack success and geometric imperceptibility. To address this issue, we propose Ortho Fusion (OF), an imperceptible 3D point cloud adversarial attack framework based on frequency-domain features and hierarchical gradient orthogonalization. The proposed method first decomposes the input point cloud into low-frequency and high-frequency components and restricts perturbation optimization to the low-frequency manifold to preserve global geometric consistency. It then employs a hierarchical asymmetric PCGrad mechanism to alleviate conflicts among full-frequency adversarial objectives, low-frequency enhancement objectives, and geometric constraints through sequential orthogonal projections. Experimental results demonstrate that OF maintains a high attack success rate while significantly improving the imperceptibility and geometric quality of adversarial examples.

title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents
abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore, as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively managing situational experience. To address this, we propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation, Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement. Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.

title: Distillation Should Be Done This Way: A Conjecture on How to Distill Knowledge-Invocation Pathways
abstract: This paper addresses the problem that, during the distillation of large language models, student models may remain at the level of imitating teacher models' answers and struggle to develop stable knowledge-invocation capabilities. It proposes a conceptual architecture for response-structure distillation and teacher–student blind-evaluation post-training, with the aim of developing transferable capabilities. This paper argues that, when two models have similar knowledge bases, differences in response quality may lie more in how knowledge is invoked, organized, and applied than in the amount of knowledge the models possess. Accordingly, this study proposes a distillation-first, training-second sequence in which the response structure is treated as an independent learning target: the student model learns the teacher model's response structures across different contexts, and then invokes its own existing knowledge to fill in those structures. Subsequently, the student model's responses are jointly evaluated through five sources of evaluation—a structure-evaluation model, a scoring model, domain experts, non-experts, and anonymous comparisons between the teacher and student models. The evaluation results and disagreements are fed back to the student model, and through repeated revision and subsequent training, the architecture attempts to gradually consolidate effective ways of invoking knowledge into stable, invocable paths within the student model. This paper further proposes mechanisms such as feeding structure-related feedback back into the revision process, limiting the number of iteration rounds, and generating training signals, so as to form a post-training closed loop of continuous correction. The proposed architecture aims to explore a possible path from imitating the teacher model's way of answering to developing the student model's own answering capabilities; its effectiveness and its ability to transfer to unseen contexts remain to be verified through subsequent experiments.

title: Reproduction package for Key-Committing Security Analysis of ACORN and Deoxys
abstract: Reproduction materials accompanying the manuscript Key-Committing Security Analysis of ACORN and Deoxys. The package provides Python construction programs, complete collision vectors, recorded verification results and computational costs, and identified reference-code sources for ACORN-128 v3, Deoxys-I-128-128 and Deoxys-II-128-128. It covers three ACORN byte-interface witnesses, including a common nonzero nonce, a nonempty message and a common associated-data prefix; and four witnesses for each Deoxys mode, including empty, full-block, partial-block and common-associated-data examples. The reference checks include both encryption and decryption for all eleven collision witnesses and eight official known-answer cases for each Deoxys mode. Execution instructions, source versions and cryptographic hashes are provided. The results concern key commitment under the input-control conditions stated in the manuscript, not conventional unknown-key AEAD security or an attack on a specific deployed protocol. The 256-bit-key Deoxys variants were not experimentally evaluated. Recorded timings are observations of the reference reproduction harness and may vary on other systems. Deoxys reference sources and their original license are included. The ACORN reference source is obtained separately from the designer's official archive using the included download-and-hash-verification helper; this retrieves exactly the files used for verification. Licensing: The MIT License applies to the independently written reproduction scripts, author-written documentation, recorded results and the local ACORN API shim. Bundled Deoxys reference programs retain GPL-2.0-or-later and their original copyright notices. The separately obtained ACORN reference source is not relicensed.

title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model–server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64–100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55–95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.

title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.

title: PAB Replication Kit v1.0: Preregistration Template, Deterministic Harness Skeleton, and Protocol Rules for Running Preregistered Adversarial Batteries Against Any System
abstract: Replication kit for the Preregistered Adversarial Batteries (PAB) protocol (methodology: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23422632). Enables any operator to run the protocol against their own system: (1) the preregistration template — falsifier table with predicted verdicts, committed before any run; (2) the deterministic harness skeleton — reference implementations of the six gate patterns (checksum/pin verification, exact-match allowlists, parity recomputation, identity-hash binding, cross-source parity, expected-count guards) plus the critical-hold gate where a refusal counts as a pass; (3) the protocol rules — seven stages, scoring criteria, hold-by-design adjudication, receipt format, and the append-only ledger discipline. Non-adaptable rules: no language model in the decision path; all injections synthetic; critical-severity events predict a fail-closed hold; misses are published as misses. The comparability contract is the frozen falsifier definition (attack class + predicted verdict), not the implementation. Published so third parties can replicate even one battery on an independent system with independent adjudication — converting the protocol from a claim into a method. This kit and its methodology are provided for educational and research purposes only. They are not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments.

title: Regional Photovoltaic Siting in Shaanxi: Integrating Ecological Value and Electricity-Demand Accessibility
abstract: Regional photovoltaic screening must reconcile land availability with ecological and electricity-demand priorities. We compared eight photovoltaic siting scenarios in Shaanxi using province-wide or regional weights derived from criterion variability and correlations. Ecological components and siting criteria, including ERA5 solar irradiation, were weighted separately. The full regional model identified 13,428.59 km2 at suitability ≥0.60. Under the separate 2872.26 km2 Top10 selection budget, adding ecological compatibility to the demand-based scenario lowered mean ecological constraint index (ECI) by 0.0883. Adding demand accessibility to the ecology-based scenario increased mean electricity-demand accessibility index (EDAI) by 0.0125. However, adding ecology raised or lowered EDAI depending on aspect treatment and resolution. The resolution comparison used a separate budget within common allowed footprints. Retrospective area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) ranged from 0.6575 to 0.6736 across the two full models and a six-factor analytic hierarchy process benchmark for 145 eligible photovoltaic polygons; paired comparisons did not resolve relative performance. Proximity grouping retained 2426.44 km2 in 929 planning groups comprising 9398 distinct physical patches. These comparisons quantify how weighting, ecological and demand criteria, and spatial representation change the land prioritized for municipal assessment.

title: Addressing symbolic obstacles in undergraduate calculus through artificial intelligence scaffolding
abstract: Symbolic obstacles in calculus prevent students from moving away from intuition and towards formal thinking, but are rarely studied in the context of artificial intelligence (AI) interaction logs. We investigated symbolic obstacles and AI-supported representational transitions among 12 Indonesian undergraduate mathematics education students in a non-intrusive intrinsic case study. Semi-structured interviews, eight classroom observations, diagnostic tests, academic artifacts, and AI logs were analyzed through inductive-deductive thematic analysis, based on Tall’s Three Worlds of Mathematics. Four obstacles are highlighted: graph-to-symbol translation, integral and sigma notation, limit notation, and symbolic algebraic manipulation. Participant-level comparisons showed 27.4%–53.8% fewer coded symbolic errors in post-activity assessments than at baseline. AI scaffolding through dynamic visualization, adaptive feedback, step-by-step guidance, and solution validation was associated with representational cycling, metacognitive reflection, reported self-efficacy gains, and lower mathematics anxiety. The study integrates AI-log evidence with the Three Worlds framework to explain how scaffolding can support students in addressing symbolic obstacles.

title: Heterogeneous graph transformer with slot-based message passing for node classification
abstract: As a widely utilized data structure, heterogeneous graphs can accurately model complex structures and multi-typed relationships, finding extensive applications in social network analysis, recommendation systems, knowledge graphs, and biomedical analysis. Node classification supports these applications by identifying entity categories or functional roles. However, during the message-passing process, mapping different types of nodes into a unified representation space often leads to cross-type feature confusion, resulting in the loss of type-specific semantic information. To address this issue, this paper proposes the HGT-Slot model. First, the model employs a type-aware Slot initialization to construct type-specific representation spaces for different node types, preserving their unique semantic attributes. Subsequently, a Slot attention mechanism is employed during the message-passing phase to preserve heterogeneous semantic information through different Slot channels. Meanwhile, the Transformer architecture is leveraged to enhance interactions among node representations, thereby improving the representation capability of the model. Finally, a Slot aggregation mechanism integrates the Slot representations for local prediction, which is fused with the global prediction from the Transformer branch for classification. Experiments on three datasets show that HGT-Slot achieves the best mean Macro-F1 and Micro-F1 scores among the compared methods for node classification.

title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
abstract: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent work has constructed anytime-valid envelopes that do, but deterministic envelopes are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each coupling a specific algorithm to a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for constructing such anytime-valid data-adaptive boundaries for a large class of iterative algorithms. Performance measures of many of these algorithms satisfy a one-step recursion that reduces the entire error analysis to a single general requirement: time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. We formalize this through a strongly adapted sub-$ψ$ condition, and derive off-the-shelf boundary constructions via continuous and discrete mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. We show how these boundaries can be directly coupled with a separate algorithmic analysis that derives the one-step recursion to provide a class of readymade anytime-valid envelopes across diverse settings including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), temporal difference learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD. In particular, for SGD, our framework either recovers or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.

title: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Entanglement Routing in Quantum Networks: Protocols, Repeater Topologies, and Co-Existence with Post-Quantum Cryptography
authors: Anish Kumar Singh, Anurag Kumar, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Vibhakar Pathak, Er. Kishan Sharma
abstract: The impending realization of fault-tolerant quantum computers threatens the foundational public-key cryptography underpinning global telecommunications and financial infrastructure. While algorithmic Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides mathematical computational hardness against quantum cryptanalysis, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) establishes an alternative information-theoretically secure physical paradigm based on the immutable laws of quantum mechanics: the No-Cloning theorem and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. However, deploying scalable, wide-area quantum networks introduces formidable physical and systems engineering challenges: exponential optical fiber attenuation that restricts direct point-to-point QKD to beneath 150 km, high dark-count rates in superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), non-deterministic Bell-state entanglement swapping across quantum repeaters, and intense Raman scattering cross-talk when multiplexing quantum channels alongside multi-terabit classical DWDM optical networks. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical architectural evaluation of quantum networking and QKD systems. We formalize the asymptotic secret key rate bounds under the Decoy-State BB84 and Measurement-Device-Independent (MDI-QKD) protocols, model continuous entanglement routing over quantum repeaters utilizing bipartite Bell-pair purification, and establish optical co-existence bounds under Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM). Furthermore, we construct an empirical optical testbed evaluating an 8-node metropolitan quantum network co-propagating QKD over 100 Gbps classical optical traffic, paired with hybrid PQC-QKD key derivation functions (ML-KEM + QKD). Our empirical findings demonstrate that decoy-state BB84 achieves a sustainable secret key rate of 1.42 kbps across 100 km of standard single-mode fiber (SMF-28), while hybrid PQC-QKD integration eliminates single-point cryptographic failures with less than 2.4 ms handshake latency overhead. Finally, we formulate open challenges in memory-assisted atomic quantum repeaters, satellite-to-ground freespace entanglement links, and quantum internet transport protocols.

title: A review of recent advances in privacy-preserving federated learning for healthcare applications
abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare, driven by the increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging systems, genomic data, and wearable devices, has created significant challenges related to patient privacy, data security, and regulatory compliance. Traditional centralised machine learning (ML) approaches often require large-scale data sharing, which increases the risk of sensitive medical information exposure. Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising distributed learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training across multiple institutions without transferring raw patient data. Recent advances in privacy-preserving FL have further strengthened its applicability in healthcare through the integration of techniques such as differential privacy (DP), homomorphic encryption (HE), secure aggregation, blockchain-assisted frameworks, and secure multi-party computation. This study critically reviews recent developments in privacy-preserving FL for healthcare applications published between 2024 and early 2026, with particular emphasis on medical imaging, EHRs analytics, genomics, and wearable health monitoring systems. In addition, major technical and security challenges, including non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data distributions, communication overhead, scalability issues, gradient leakage, model poisoning, and membership inference attacks, are comprehensively analysed. Regulatory, ethical, and interoperability concerns associated with cross-institutional collaboration are also discussed. Finally, current research gaps, emerging trends, and future directions for developing secure, scalable, and trustworthy federated healthcare systems are identified.

title: From Adult Renal Masses to Pediatric Wilms Tumors: Evaluating Cross-Domain Generalization of Kidney Lesion Segmentation on MRI
authors: Alida F. W. van der Steeg
abstract: Deep learning segmentation models for pediatric oncology are often trained on small, single-center cohorts, whereas much larger datasets exist for adult diseases, such as kidney cancer. Whether models trained on adult renal lesions generalize to pediatric Wilms tumors remains unclear. We trained a segmentation model on single-sequence T1- or T2-weighted adult kidney MRI and evaluated it on a held-out adult test set and a pediatric Wilms tumor cohort, where it was compared with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net. Segmentation performance was quantified using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. On the adult test set, the model achieved a median DSC of 0.86 for renal lesions. On the pediatric cohort, the adult-trained model achieved a median DSC of 0.85 compared with 0.90 for the pediatric-specific model. Despite differences in age, anatomy, and tumor type, the adult-trained model showed promising performance on pediatric Wilms tumors, with only a modest difference in median DSC compared with the pediatric-specific model. However, non-inferiority could not be shown, highlighting the value of pediatric training data. In future work, a fine-tuning strategy could be explored.

title: The Reasoning Stack Manager: Governed, Chunked Reasoning for Stateless and Small Language Models — An Implementation Report under LMCP and PSOS
abstract: An implementation report under LMCP and PSOS. The Reasoning Stack Manager drives stateless and small language models through bounded work. It holds reasoning as a resumable graph and a context ledger outside the prompt. Twelve deterministic gates score every call, and a reaper recovers by failure class, bounded by progress rather than time. The harness, not the model, decides whether done is earned.Work is chunked to what one reply of the specific model can carry. A task that stalls is decomposed into chained ledger tasks that any capable worker pulls: the "chunk swarm", designed for FluxBox appliances running open models at 1-3 tokens per second.Results: in a controlled pilot, 3B and 7B models answered two call-site investigations to ground truth in 2 calls and about 490 input tokens. In six days of production, input tokens per completed task fell 64-74% for the same cloud models. An independent verifier confirmed only 6 of 28 checked done claims, and the report treats this as the main open problem. Includes FluxBox model evaluations (code-change replay, chapter extraction, live task classes, throughput) and proposed requirements R-d to R-j for the next drafts of LMCP and PSOS.Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Companion reports: Harness-Driven Progressive Detail (10.6084/m9.figshare.34052538) and Ledger-Derived Memory (10.6084/m9.figshare.34052541).

title: Quantum Teleportation: Perfect State Transfer via Entanglement, Not Matter — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: Quantum teleportation is a protocol for transferring an unknown quantum state via shared entanglement and classical communication — not a transport of matter or energy. | MATH: The protocol relies on the Bell basis: |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, |Ψ⁺⟩ = (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2, and the Pauli corrections {I, X, Z, XZ} applied after a two-qubit Bell measurement. The state transfer fidelity is 1 (perfect) in ideal conditions, requiring 2 classical bits per teleported qubit (no-cloning theorem preserved). | CONNECTION: The Bell states form an orthonormal basis in ℂ²⊗ℂ² — a 4-dimensional space whose symmetry group is the Clifford group, related to the root system D₄ (the 24-cell, a 4D crystallographic polytope with 24 vertices). The coefficients 1/√2 = 0.7071 appear, and the ratio of the number of classical bits (2) to quantum bits (1) is 2:1 — a binary harmonic, not directly golden. However, the entanglement entropy of a Bell state is ln(2) = 0.6931 nats, close to 0.7071 but not equal. No dire Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Integrating Deep Learning and Knowledge Graphs for Natural Language Inference
abstract: Natural Language Inference (NLI) deals with the problem of logical entailment between two sentences. It is evidenced that apart from interpretation of words and syntactic structures, use of external relevant knowledge is also required. This paper investigates whether the integration of external knowledge, represented as triplets and extracted from Knowledge Graphs (KGs), can improve the performance of a pretrained language model on NLI tasks. It also investigates how the source of knowledge affects performance. Six benchmark datasets, namely RTE, QNLI, SICK, SNLI, DNLI, and SciTail, were enriched with knowledge extracted from AristoTuple and WordNet, while ConceptNet was additionally used for the SNLI and SciTail datasets. Enrichment was applied only to the training data through a strict relevance-based selection mechanism using paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and cosine-similarity filtering, and the resulting datasets were used to fine-tune BERT-base-uncased. Evaluation included method-specific configurations selected through validation-based hyperparameter exploration and a controlled multi-seed setting using the vanilla baseline hyperparameters with matched seeds across baseline and enriched datasets. The best observed validation accuracy was 95.24% on SciTail with AristoTuple, while the highest test accuracy, also on SciTail, was 93.70% with ConceptNet. Across both evaluation settings, the effect of knowledge enrichment varied across datasets and knowledge sources, with the multi-seed analysis further assessing the robustness of these effects under controlled training conditions. Overall, the proposed data-level approach achieved competitive performance compared with more complex knowledge-enhanced NLI methods. A taxonomy of existing NLI approaches is also presented.

title: Beyond Expected Values: Risk-Sensitive Planning with Distributional Monte-Carlo Tree Search
abstract: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) typically stores only scalar mean estimates, which makes it poorly suited for tail-risk objectives such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR). We introduce Categorical Thompson Sampling with Optimism (CATSO) and Particle Thompson Sampling with Optimism (PATSO), two distributional MCTS algorithms that maintain finite-support empirical backup laws at Q-edges. CATSO represents Q-edge laws with categorical atoms and Dirichlet Thompson sampling, while PATSO represents them with adaptive particles. Both algorithms select actions using the CVaR of a Thompson-sampled Q-edge law plus a polynomial optimism bonus, and propagate scalar continuation values through visit-weighted averages of child Q-edge CVaR scores. For the finite-depth nested CVaR planning target, we prove an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the root value error after $n$ rollouts, which upper-bounds the risk-sensitive simple regret. CATSO adds a fixed-grid discretization bias, while capped PATSO adds a tunable Wasserstein compression bias. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show that distributional Q-edges improve lower-tail return and reduce catastrophic outcomes when mean-optimal and risk-sensitive behavior differ.

title: CMD: A Fail-Closed, Machine-Checked Verdict for Silent Microarchitectural Divergence on a Verified Replay Substrate
abstract: What this record is. Version 1 of the CMD preprint and its companion artifact. This version contains the parts of the work that are finished and checkable today: the formal development (machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL, trust base of exactly two axioms asserted at build time), the on-box reducer and host-side transport driver with their test suites, the system design, and a buildability experiment for the fine measurement surface. It also fixes, in public and with a timestamp, the protocol of the in-VMM measurement campaign that the final paper will report (Sec. VI-B of the PDF). That campaign has not been run; this record contains no in-VMM measurement and makes no empirical claim about detection. What CMD is. CMD issues a verdict about one replay pair — an execution and its counterfactual replay on the EXTp substrate (seL4). The verdict's meaning is a theorem: a CMD fire implies that the pair is indistinguishable on the coarse surface the defender observes (VM-exit tuple and timing, at EXTp's calibrated threshold) and distinguishable on a fine surface the defender does not (a hardware performance-counter reading, at its own calibrated threshold). CMD maps observational blindness; it does not claim to detect attacks, and a fine-surface divergence is not yet a channel. What is proved here. Both clauses of the verdict are instances of one sound-reduction scheme, proved once; the two instances differ only in polarity and round their thresholds in opposite directions. The verdict is computed on the box in exact 128-bit integer arithmetic and carried across a machine reset through CMOS NVRAM by a fail-closed protocol whose soundness needs transport integrity only. Abstract lift theorems separate what a sound detector can and cannot conclude (soundness of the fine surface is insufficient; completeness is the obligation). What is measured here. One buildability experiment, with its protocol fixed before the first run (prereg.json in the artifact; no earlier public timestamp exists, so it is not called pre-registered): the fine surface resolves two workloads with identical architectural output and timing that differs by construction, with a separation about five orders of magnitude above the noise floor, in three independent boots of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C (Ice Lake-SP) server. Every measured number in the PDF names the CPU it was taken on. The EXTp calibration numbers quoted from the prior work belong to EXTp's Alder Lake machine and will be re-measured on the campaign CPU. What is pending (and why this is published now). The in-VMM campaign — recalibration on the final CPU, the fine-surface threshold, a mandatory zero-effect intervention control (the intervention path executed with x′ = x, to bound the instrument's own effect on the counter), cross-boot false-positive rates, overhead, an end-to-end fire, and a Training Solo case study — is scheduled next. This version is published to date the formal results and to fix the campaign protocol before any campaign data exist. A later version of this record will add the measurements; the version history is the audit trail. Artifact. CMD_artifact_v1.zip: Isabelle sources and ROOT (isabelle build -D isabelle), reducer and driver with tests, the threshold-table generator and its independent 50-digit recomputation, the buildability-experiment harness, its three session reports and the machine record (world.json), and this PDF. The seL4 VMM itself is part of the EXTp artifact (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23403670) and is not duplicated.

title: Why Enterprise AI Projects Fail After POC Success
abstract: We celebrated our ML proof-of-concept like shipping a product. 94% accuracy. Board demo. Six months later: nobody used it. Forrester's data shows this is the norm—61% of enterprise AI pilots succeed, then stall. Here's why pilots and production are fundamentally different problems. Full article: https://davidohnstad.net/why-enterprise-ai-projects-fail-after-poc/

title: Event-Anchored Fusion Ancestry and Consumer-Adequate Continuations
abstract: This paper specifies an event-anchored consumer for labelled single-defect circular actions. The consumer requests the origin of a selected fusion, its later carrier absorptions, the current placed partition, and the legal domains and successors of continuation commands.On singleton-seed-generated domains, a finite placed-fusion forest recovers the complete consumer state and preserves it through every legal finite continuation. A placed forward union-find-with-explanations adapter provides a second realization. The results establish sufficiency for this declared consumer, not minimality, efficiency, or machine verification of the general theorems. Bounded replay and partial Lean formalization are provided as supporting controls. Source repository: https://github.com/dooven-prime/rime-lite. Paper XXXIX of the Representation-Induced Mechanics and Evolution (RIME) program. Independent researcher; no institutional affiliation.

title: LiveSync: Iterative Self-Training for Lip-Sync Generation
abstract: Audio-driven lip synchronization aims to match target speech through localized mouth and jaw articulation while preserving subject identity, head pose, and surrounding facial context. Naturally recorded videos provide synchronized reconstruction targets but rarely offer pairs that are matched in identity and pose yet differ primarily in speech-related articulation. Mask-based training enables reconstruction from these videos, but random-reference inputs differ from the aligned self-reference used at inference. We present LiveSync, an iterative self-training framework in which a single mask-based model generates pseudo pairs and is refined for deployment. The model is first trained on a curated real-video corpus augmented with externally generated clips covering under-represented visual conditions. title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.
